summary: Chatham Light at the elbow of Cape Cod: twin wooden towers from 1808, erosion moved the station in 1877, one tower moved to Nauset in 1923, and the 1877 cast-iron tower still stands.

lens.where: outside the Atwood House Museum, Chatham Historical Society (removed from the tower in 1969)

structures.note: Twin octagonal towers about 40 feet high on movable skids, placed 70 feet apart (LighthouseFriends; marker).
Rebuilt in brick, $6,750 (LighthouseFriends; marker). Abandoned after the 1877 move; the south tower fell to the beach in December 1878 (or 1879), the north tower about fifteen months later.
Built across the road from the old site. 48 feet (NRHP, 1877 tower); the marker says 44 feet. Rings bolted together and lined with brick (LighthouseFriends). Replacement lantern 1969.
Double keeper's house built with the 1877 towers; a door connecting the halves was cut in 1881 (LighthouseFriends; NRHP).
Oil house, white brick with slate roof and cupola (NRHP).

access.note: The light complex is headquarters for Coast Guard Station Chatham (marker). Treat the buildings as working Coast Guard property.

events.note: Congress makes its first appropriation for a lighthouse at Chatham (marker)
Twin wooden towers and keeper's house completed (marker)
Samuel Nye appointed by President Jefferson, 7 October 1808 (LighthouseFriends; marker)
Wooden towers torn down and rebuilt in brick for $6,750 (LighthouseFriends; marker)
Fourth-order Fresnel lenses with lard-oil lamps installed (LighthouseFriends; marker)
Position of assistant keeper added to the station (LighthouseFriends)
Erosion prompts a new station across the road; cast-iron towers and double dwelling built
Fresnel lenses moved into the new towers and lit on 6 September 1877 (LighthouseFriends)
South tower plummets to the beach, 15 December 1878 (LighthouseFriends). The marker gives 15 December 1879.
North tower and 1841 keeper's house follow about fifteen months after the south tower (approximate year; sources differ)
Door cut between the halves of the double dwelling
Life-Saving Service Station No. 13 moved about two miles north of the Chatham lights because of encroachment of the sea (not the light station itself)
North tower moved to Nauset Beach (Nauset Light); Chatham twin light discontinued (Lighthouse Service Bulletin 1932)
Fourth-order L. Sautter Fresnel lens with clockwork drive and incandescent oil-vapor lamp in the south tower
Electric motor replaces clockwork; intensity increased from 30,000 to 800,000 candlepower
Tanker Pendelton broke in two during a snowstorm, 18 February 1952; rescued by Station Chatham, whose headquarters is in the light complex
Fresnel lens and lantern room removed to the Atwood House Museum; larger lantern with aerobeacon installed
Listed on the National Register on 15 June 1987
New DCB-224 aerobeacons installed (LighthouseFriends, August 1993; the marker gives 1994)

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record gives the cast-iron tower a build date of 1808. The 1808 towers were wooden; the cast-iron towers were built in 1877 (NRHP; LighthouseFriends; marker).
The marker says the 1923 north light went to Eastham; LighthouseFriends and the NRHP say Nauset Beach. Nauset Light stands in Eastham, so these agree on the place.

notes_for_editor: Newspaper search was not attempted for Chatham (loc.gov was returning HTTP 520 for every query in this run). The USCG Historian's Chatham page could not be read (archive copies returned only a frame). LighthouseFriends is copyrighted: facts restated, and at most one short quotation per story. The marker's text is a community database entry; its dates and figures are cited as the marker gives them. Conflicts for a reviewer: (a) Stinson's end year (LighthouseFriends: resigned 1839, and its own keeper list gives Lot Norton 1839-1841; the USLHS roster keeps Stinson to 1841 and names no Norton; the story states both, and the Norton line is in keepers with cite 1 only); (b) south tower collapse 15 December 1878 (LighthouseFriends) or 1879 (marker); (c) Hardy's end year 1899 (roster, LighthouseFriends) or 1900 (marker); (d) cast-iron tower height 48 ft (NRHP) or 44 ft (marker); (e) Woodman and Allison end years (Allison 1927 in the roster and LighthouseFriends, 1928 in some secondary sources not cited here); (f) lens and lantern removal 1969 and aerobeacon date 1993 (LighthouseFriends) or 1994 (marker). The record's range of 14 nm conflicts with the marker's 24 nautical miles for the present light; the 24 nm figure is proposed as a correction for the present optic. The record's first_lit 1808 rests on the marker's completion date of 1808; no source checked here gives a lighting date. The Life-Saving Service Station No. 13 is mentioned only because a source ties its move to the lights; it is a separate station. The 1952 Pendleton rescue crew is not named. Keepers and staff named from the roster are historical, and none postdates 1960 except Woodman's and Gustavus's end years, which fall before 1960.

corrections.why: The present cast-iron tower dates from 1877. The 1808 towers were wooden twin towers that were rebuilt in brick in 1841 and then replaced.
The marker gives 24 nautical miles for the present light (installed 1993-1994). The record's 14 nm is not supported by any source checked here.
